B07_00: This growth factor signal controls epithelial cell scattering, wound closure and invasive growth by acting at the sites where cells grip their surroundings, setting how fast and in which direction they migrate. It matters for tissue repair and is especially relevant in carcinomas, where its heightened activity accompanies invasion and metastasis rather than simply proliferation.
B07_01: Co-receptors on endothelial cells tune their responsiveness to vascular growth factors during the growth of blood and lymphatic vessels, with one form favouring arteries and angiogenic vessels and the other veins and lymphatics. Loss of their function disrupts vascular patterning in the embryo. The same interface is exploited in tumour angiogenesis and is a target of anti-angiogenic cancer strategies.
B07_02: Epithelial cells respond to growth factors with proliferation, migration and changes in cell shape, and this branch of the response contributes to renewal and repair of skin, gut and other epithelia. Inappropriate output from it contributes to the growth and invasiveness of carcinomas driven by overactive growth factor receptors, such as some lung, head and neck and breast cancers.
B07_03: Endothelial cells divide in response to vascular growth signals, the basis of new blood vessel formation during development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation. This proliferative response is the target of anti-angiogenic drugs used against cancer and against eye diseases with abnormal vessel growth. The same signalling also supports endothelial survival, helping to maintain existing vessels.
B07_04: This growth factor response supports epithelial cell survival, motility and tissue regeneration in organs such as liver, kidney and skin. It is a principal reason tumours driven by this receptor resist cell death and invade. Amplification or activating mutation of the receptor, or excess growth factor supplied by surrounding stroma, keeps the signal on, and this is targeted by kinase inhibitor drugs.
B07_05: This growth factor receptor converts signals into changes in gene expression in several tissues. In neural precursor cells it suppresses the formation of astrocytes, during lactation it promotes milk protein production in the mammary gland, and it influences hormone responsiveness in breast tissue. Its activity is therefore linked to mammary differentiation and to breast cancer behaviour.
B07_06: Shutting down this growth factor receptor sets how much signal cells convert into proliferation, differentiation or gene regulation. Excessive or unopposed signalling contributes to tumour growth, while appropriate restraint shapes development of the heart and nervous system, where the receptor acts. Its turnover thus links growth control in development to cancer.
B07_07: This is the canonical textbook route by which a growth factor at the surface of an epithelial cell drives proliferation and survival. Because the link is so direct, activating mutations in the receptor or its downstream switch drive lung, colorectal and other carcinomas. These mutations determine whether receptor-blocking therapy can work, making this step central to treatment selection in cancer.
B07_08: Beyond driving proliferation, this growth factor receptor family steers where epithelial cells move, supporting wound closure and tissue morphogenesis by establishing cell polarity and directed migration. In breast cancers with an amplified receptor, hyperactivation of this motility arm contributes to invasion and metastasis rather than growth alone, making it relevant to tumour spread.
B07_09: Blood and lymphatic vessels grow where endothelial cells receive growth factor signals, and this initiating step drives endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vessel permeability. It is how tumours recruit their own blood supply and is the target of anti-angiogenic drugs. Its dysregulation underlies vascular malformations, lymphoedema and pathological vessel growth in retinopathy and cancer.
B07_10: This survival branch of growth factor signalling operates in the nervous system, heart and mammary epithelium, guiding neuronal migration, synapse formation, heart muscle maturation and lactational differentiation. Its disruption has been linked to cardiomyopathy and to schizophrenia risk. Whether a given cell uses this branch depends on which receptor variant it makes, so tissues differ in their survival responses.
B07_11: Activation of this growth factor receptor drives epithelial survival, scattering, motility and branching morphogenesis, underpinning liver and placental development, wound repair and tissue regeneration. How much active growth factor is available is controlled outside the cell, setting the strength of the response in injured tissue. Excessive activation is a recurrent driver of invasive carcinoma.
B07_12: This growth factor makes epithelial cells move only when they are also attached to the surrounding matrix, coupling a soluble cue to the adhesive state of the cell. It supports wound re-epithelialisation and branching morphogenesis during development. The same axis drives invasion and metastasis in carcinomas where the receptor is amplified or the growth factor is supplied by tumour stroma.
B07_13: How long and how strongly an epithelial cell responds to this growth factor depends on where the activated receptor travels inside the cell after uptake. Sustained responses support the motility, scattering and invasive growth of epithelial cells, which carcinomas hijack during progression. This trafficking step thus acts as a control point on signal duration in tissue repair and cancer.
B07_14: This branch links a growth factor at the epithelial cell surface to changes in gene expression that drive scattering, morphogenesis and invasive growth. Its output, growth without anchorage and increased motility, is why it is scrutinised in carcinomas where the receptor is amplified or the tumour makes its own growth factor. Normally it supports epithelial repair, liver regeneration and branching morphogenesis.
B07_15: This negative feedback limits how long growth signals last in epithelial cells by controlling how much receptor remains at the cell surface. When the brake is weak, cells become more sensitive to growth factors. Loss of this brake contributes to sustained survival signalling in breast and other epithelial cancers and is one route to resistance against receptor-targeted therapy.
B07_16: Growth factor receptors must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this removal limits the strength and duration of growth signalling in epithelial cells. Loss of this braking system leaves the receptor chronically active, a route to transformation exploited by many epithelial tumours, so it is an important safeguard against cancer.
B07_17: This branch of growth factor signalling steers epithelial cells toward migration and secretion rather than simple proliferation. It contributes to the invasive behaviour of breast tumours with receptor amplification. Because it depends on which receptor partners pair up, it illustrates how the receptor make-up of a normal or cancerous cell determines the kind of response a growth signal produces.
B07_18: This branch makes epithelial cells scatter, spread, adhere and move, processes used in wound healing, liver regeneration and embryonic morphogenesis. Carcinomas hijack it for invasion and metastasis, and sustained activity through this axis is a feature of tumours with an amplified receptor, linking growth factor signalling to cancer spread.
B07_19: Much of this growth factor's effect on epithelial proliferation, survival, scattering and morphogenesis runs through this branch, which reprogrammes gene expression for motility and growth. Constitutive activity, caused by receptor amplification or mutation, sustains invasive growth in carcinomas and is a target of kinase inhibitor therapy.
B07_20: Amplification of this receptor drives an aggressive subset of breast and gastric cancers, and blocking it with small-molecule kinase inhibitors or therapeutic antibodies is one of the clearest successes of targeted cancer therapy. Treatment removes proliferative and survival signals from tumour cells. Resistance commonly arises through mutation of the receptor or bypass activation of related receptors.
B07_21: This growth factor receptor drives scattering, motility, invasive growth and survival, and becomes oncogenic when amplified or mutated in solid tumours. Its activation also emerges as an escape route in tumours treated with drugs against related receptors. Blocking it with antibodies or kinase inhibitors therefore matters both as primary cancer therapy and as a way to overcome acquired resistance.
B07_22: This branch supports proliferation, survival and differentiation in neural, cardiac and mammary tissue, where the growth factor signal shapes synapse formation, heart development and lactational differentiation. Disturbance of the axis is linked to susceptibility to schizophrenia and to breast cancer, making it relevant to both neurodevelopmental and oncological disease.
B07_23: After a cell has responded to the hormone that lowers blood sugar, it must destroy the hormone and return its receptor to the surface. This sets how long a cell stays responsive and how quickly the circulating hormone is cleared, mainly in liver and other target tissues. It therefore bears directly on hormone sensitivity and on the resistance seen in type 2 diabetes.
B07_24: This step converts growth factor binding into proliferation and serves epithelial growth, cardiac and neural development, and wound repair. In breast and gastric cancers with receptor amplification, it is a principal route by which tumours sustain constant proliferative signalling, and mutation of downstream components underlies resistance to receptor-targeted therapy.
B07_25: This is the principal growth-promoting output of a key epithelial growth factor receptor, driving proliferation, survival and migration of epithelial cells in skin, gut and other tissues. Activating mutations in the receptor or its downstream switch lock it on and are among the commonest drivers of lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers.
B07_26: This kinase link connects growth factor receptor engagement to the proliferation, migration and survival of epithelial cells. It matters in breast cancer, where receptor amplification and high levels of the kinase occur together, reinforcing tumour growth and contributing to resistance against receptor-targeted therapy. Signals that seem to come from related receptors may be relayed through the same route.
B07_27: This branch of growth factor signalling links receptor activation to proliferation and migration of epithelial cells. It matters clinically because the adaptor gene sits beside the receptor gene on chromosome 17 and is co-amplified with it in breast cancer, coupling receptor overexpression to invasive behaviour as well as growth. Its downstream effects remain incompletely defined.
B07_28: This route drives proliferation and survival in epithelial, cardiac and neural tissues in response to growth factors. In breast and gastric cancers with amplification of the receptor involved, it becomes a major oncogenic output and therefore a drug target. Its strength and duration are fine-tuned, shaping how strongly normal and tumour tissues respond to growth signals.
B07_29: When vascular growth factor acts on endothelium, blood vessels dilate and become leaky, letting plasma proteins escape into the tissues. This loosening provides the space and matrix into which new vessels sprout, so it is an early step in angiogenesis. It is also the basis of oedema in tumours, diabetic retinopathy and inflammation.
B07_30: After a pulse of the hormone that lowers blood sugar, cells must return to baseline, and this attenuation step switches off the response. It keeps blood sugar control responsive to hormonal cues. Loss of the shutdown leaves growth and metabolic signalling running without a hormonal cue, whereas excessive attenuation blunts hormone action and contributes to insulin resistance.
B07_31: This survival branch of growth factor signalling promotes cell survival, growth and metabolic activity in epithelial tissues. It matters clinically because receptor amplification in breast and gastric cancer, together with common activating mutations further down the pathway, makes tumour cells dependent on it for survival and shapes their response to receptor-directed therapy.
B07_32: This step lets epithelial cells respond to growth factors with proliferation and resistance to cell death, and connects growth signalling to cell adhesion. Excessive flux through it is a recurring feature of cancers driven by overactive growth factor receptors, such as some lung carcinomas, where it supports tumour survival and growth.
B07_33: This branch contributes to epithelial cell scattering, motility, wound repair and morphogenesis in response to a growth factor. The same axis is hijacked in carcinomas where the receptor is amplified or mutated. Because it both propagates and limits the signal, it helps set how strongly epithelial cells proliferate and migrate in normal tissue repair and in cancer.
B07_34: This step couples hormone binding to sugar uptake by muscle and fat, storage of energy reserves in liver and muscle, and growth and gene expression throughout the body. It is the main point at which metabolic signalling is tuned. Its loss or inactivation underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, linking it to obesity-related metabolic disease.
